newsitem.title: CHINA: China claims credit for Hong Kong's prosperity.
newsitem.headline: China claims credit for Hong Kong's prosperity.

text.p: China claimed credit on Wednesday for Hong Kong's prosperity and stability, saying a decision not to invade the British colony when the communists swept to power in 1949 was a crucial factor.

In a front-page story, the official People's Daily said China has been a "strong backup" to Hong Kong, providing the territory ceded to Britain after the 19th century opium wars with food and water for decades.

The People's Daily credited Hong Kong's prosperity to a decision by the late Communist Party Chairman Mao Zedong not to invade the enclave and take it back after the Communists won the Chinese civil war in 1949.
"This arrangement by Chairman Mao Zedong...was to break through isolation imposed by the Western bloc and leave a bridge and ventilated window to the outside," the newspaper said.
The People's Daily said China has given Hong Kong business a competitive edge over foreign competition, providing cheap land, labour and raw materials, and the world's largest market.

The article is the third in a series published in the mouthpiece of the ruling Communist Party to mark the return of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Hong Kong investors poured $99.3 billion into China from 1979 to 1995, accounting for 60 percent of total foreign investment, the newspaper said. China is Hong Kong's biggest export market, it said.
The newspaper ignored Britain's contributions to Hong Kong's prosperity.
It said China's policy toward Hong Kong had not wavered even during "fierce political movements" on the mainland.

The catastrophic ultra-leftist 1966-76 Cultural Revolution left China in shambles with schools closed, families broken up and members banished to the countryside while radical Red Guards destroyed temples and works of art. Hong Kong was virtually unscathed, apart from China-backed riots in 1967.

China also purged hundreds of thousands of intellectuals during the Anti-Rightist Movement in 1957 after they were encouraged to criticise the Communist Party in the "Hundred Flowers Bloom" campaign. Hong Kong was not affected.
Hong Kong would not be what it is today without China, the newspaper said.
"It would be difficult for Hong Kong to soar if it did not have a stable and reliable backing," the People's Daily said.
"For decades, the motherland has always been endeavouring to create a prosperous and stable Hong Kong," it said.
China currently supplies Hong Kong with 70 percent of its annual water needs, or 1.1 billion cubic metres.
"This is the water of life... It's difficult to imagine what Hong Kong would be like today if it had no water," it said.
"Hong Kong's prosperity and stability cannot do without the motherland's support," the People's Daily said.
The newspaper said Hong Kong has been a free port since the 1840s, but its economy did not take off until 20 years ago -- implying that China had been essential to Hong Kong's boom.
China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping launched market reforms and began opening China to the outside world in 1979, three years after the Cultural Revolution ended with Mao's death.
